1240.title: Was anything ever born?
1240.hook: seed or sprout, chicken or egg? Gaudapada answers that nothing was ever truly born, and no one truly bound
1240.carry: ajati: no one was ever truly bound
1240.tomorrow: Emptying the sea with a blade of grass
1240.howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta meet Gaudapada's teaching of ajati by reading the Karika, often with a teacher and with Shankara's commentary.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Karika, the rope in the dark: the snake never went anywhere, because it was never apart from the rope.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: ROPE OR SNAKE?`

segments.voice: The argument starts over dessert. Which came first, the chicken or the egg? Somebody says the chicken, obviously; something had to lay it. Somebody else says the egg, obviously; the chicken hatched from one. An uncle says it's a trick question. Nobody wins, and everybody has a good time. Thinkers in India argued over the same kind of loop with a seed and a sprout: the seed makes the sprout, the sprout makes the seed. Gaudapada picks up that puzzle in the Mandukya Karika. But he doesn't pick a side. He asks whether anything was ever really born at all.
screen: `THE CHICKEN OR THE EGG?` → `SEED AND SPROUT.` → `WAS ANYTHING EVER BORN?`

segments.voice: The word is ajati. Jati means birth; a-jati means no birth, non-origination. Here's how Gaudapada gets there. Try to explain how something comes to be. Does it come from something that already exists? Then it didn't really come to be; it was already there. Does it come from what doesn't exist at all? Nothing comes from nothing. Cause and effect chasing each other, like seed and sprout, never find a first beginning. So, he says, the wise don't affirm birth. Then a stark verse: there is no dissolution and no origination; no one bound, no one striving, no one seeking freedom, no one freed. That, he says, is the highest truth. It can sound cold the first time. No one freed, after all this seeking? But look at it from yesterday's path. When the rope is seen, the snake isn't killed. Nothing is destroyed, nothing is saved; the danger was simply never born. Gaudapada also says why the scriptures describe creation at all: stories of the world coming forth, like sparks from a fire or pots from clay, lead the mind toward the truth; they aren't the last word on it. That's a bold claim, and it's his. Some other Vedanta schools hold that creation is real, that the Lord truly brings the world forth, and they answer him with care. So why would a Hindu seeker care? The goal of the path is moksha, freedom. On Gaudapada's reading, moksha isn't something new you manufacture, a prize born on the day you finally earn it. If no one was ever truly bound, freedom is recognizing what was always so.
screen: `AJATI: NO BIRTH.` · `NOT FROM BEING, NOT FROM NOTHING.` · `NO ONE BOUND, NO ONE FREED.` · `CREATION STORIES LEAD THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Let the mind be as it is, and when a thought appears, a plan, a memory, a tune, gently ask: where did it start? Don't chase an answer; just look for its first moment, then let it go and wait for the next. If you pray, rest in what was here before any thought.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, carrying his teaching of ajati: on his reading, nothing at all is ever truly born.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ajati: no one was ever truly bound. On Gaudapada's reading, freedom is seeing what was always so. Same time tomorrow.

1241.title: Emptying the sea with a blade of grass
1241.hook: one blade of grass, dipped in the sea, one drop at a time, until the sea is empty. Gaudapada uses that picture for steadying the mind
1241.carry: asparsha yoga: steady the mind, grasp at nothing
1241.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, meditation is practiced alongside study and reflection, and Gaudapada's verses on steadying the mind are read as guidance for it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Mandukya Karika, ajati, no birth: no one bound, no one freed, and a danger that was never born.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: AJATI, NO BIRTH.`

segments.voice: One blade of grass. Dip its tip in the sea. Lift it. One drop hangs there, shining, and falls onto the sand. Dip it again. Another drop. Now keep going, without hurry and without giving up, until the sea is empty. It sounds like a riddle, or a punishment from an old story. It's neither. It's a line from the Mandukya Karika, and Gaudapada isn't joking. He's describing how to steady a mind, and he says it takes exactly that kind of patience.
screen: `A BLADE OF GRASS, THE SEA.` → `ONE DROP AT A TIME.` → `THE PATIENCE OF STEADYING A MIND.`

segments.voice: It would be easy to think Gaudapada has nothing to say about practice. He does. He names a discipline asparsha yoga, the yoga of no contact, meaning no grasping, no clinging to what appears. And he admits it's hard. Even yogis, he says, are afraid of it; they see fear where there's nothing to fear. Then the image: the mind is to be steadied without growing weary, the way someone might empty the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of grass. The point isn't that the task can be finished by Tuesday. It's the kind of effort: tireless, unhurried, not discouraged. Then he gets specific, almost like a coach. When the mind drifts toward dullness and sleep, wake it. When it's scattered, bring it back to calm. When it's caught in desire, know that it's caught. When it's resting in balance, don't disturb it. And a warning that surprises some readers: don't sit and savor the happiness that comes in deep stillness. Stay unattached, through clear seeing. Even the sweet part isn't something to grab. This fits the rest of the Karika. If nothing is truly born, the practice isn't building something new. It's the patient undoing of grasping, until the mind, in his words elsewhere, stops imagining and comes to rest. This is dhyana, meditation, as Gaudapada teaches it: not one heroic sitting that empties the mind, but coming back, again and again, without weariness. His instructions are humble ones: wake it, calm it, notice it, leave it be.
screen: `ASPARSHA: THE YOGA OF NO CONTACT.` · `THE OCEAN AND A BLADE OF GRASS.` · `WAKE IT, CALM IT, NOTICE, LEAVE IT.` · `DON'T SAVOR EVEN THE STILLNESS.`

segments.voice: Try Gaudapada's four small moves. If the mind gets drowsy, sit up a little and open your attention; if it scatters, come back to one breath. If it reaches for something, a plan or a craving, just notice: caught; and if it rests, let it rest, without holding on to the rest. If you pray, let each return be an offering.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, with their patient practice: steadying the mind like emptying the ocean with a blade of grass.

segments.voice: Your line: asparsha yoga: steady the mind, grasp at nothing. One drop at a time, without growing weary. Until tomorrow.

1242.title: The space inside the pot
1242.hook: an empty clay pot holds a little piece of sky. Gaudapada asks what happens to that sky when the pot breaks
1242.carry: atman is like space: one, never cut apart
1242.howItsDone: Students of Advaita Vedanta often read the Mandukya Karika with Shankara's commentary under a teacher, and the image of space in a pot is still used in talks and classes to point to the self.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika's practical verses: steady the mind like emptying the ocean with a blade of grass, tireless and unhurried.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: A BLADE OF GRASS AND THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: An empty clay pot sits on a kitchen shelf. Empty, we say. But inside it is space, a small round piece of the same open space that fills the kitchen, the street, the sky over the house. Pour water in and the water takes up that space. Pour it out and the space is still there, shaped like the pot. Now drop the pot. It shatters. Where did the space inside it go? It didn't fly anywhere. It didn't break. It just stopped looking separate. Gaudapada uses exactly this picture in the Mandukya Karika.
screen: `AN EMPTY POT ON A SHELF.` → `A PIECE OF THE SAME SPACE.` → `THE POT BREAKS. WHERE DID IT GO?`

segments.voice: In the Karika's section called Advaita, not-two, Gaudapada says the self, atman, is like space, and living beings, each of us, are like the space inside pots. The pots seem to make many small spaces out of one. When the pots break, he says, the space in each merges back into space. So it is with living beings and the self. Then he answers the obvious objection: if we're all one self, why does one person suffer while another is happy? His reply stays with the pots. If the space in one pot is filled with dust and smoke, the space in every other pot isn't dirty. One person's joy or grief doesn't spill into all the others. Forms differ, uses differ, names differ, he says, yet space itself is not divided. Other Vedanta schools read the self and living beings as truly distinct, and answer this image in their own way. Gaudapada adds a careful line. The space in the pot is not a piece cut out of space, and not something space turned into. Just so, a living being is not a part of the self or a change in it. Last: to children, he says, the sky can look dirty. The dirt is in the seeing, not in the sky. So the self only seems stained to those who don't yet see clearly. The smoke drifts, the pot breaks, and the sky was never touched. That's the Advaita teaching in one picture: one self in every being. And one self isn't one mood: your grief is still yours; the space it sits in isn't divided.
screen: `THE SELF IS LIKE SPACE.` · `SMOKE IN ONE POT, NOT IN ALL.` · `NOT A PIECE, NOT A CHANGE.` · `THE DIRT IS IN THE SEEING.`

segments.voice: Look at a cup or a bowl near you and notice the space inside it, then the space around it, then the room's space running out through a window or a door. Close your eyes if you like and rest in that openness; when a thought arrives, let it be smoke in one pot, which doesn't change the space. If you pray, you can rest there as an offering.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where the self is pictured as open space, and each life as space held for a while inside a pot.

segments.voice: Your line: atman is like space: one, never cut apart. Smoke in one pot never stains the sky. See you tomorrow.

1243.title: The torch held still
1243.hook: a sparkler whirled in the dark draws circles that aren't there. the Karika's last section: the firebrand, held still
1243.carry: the world is consciousness moving, like a whirled torch
1243.tomorrow: The first hymn is to fire
1243.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya Upanishad is often studied together with Gaudapada's Karika and Shankara's commentary on both, and the firebrand image is used by teachers to point to consciousness behind the movement of the mind.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika and the space inside a pot: smoke in one pot doesn't dirty the rest, and the sky was never touched.
screen: `THE SPACE IN THE POT.`

segments.voice: A backyard after dark, and a kid with a sparkler. She swings it fast, and a ring of light hangs in the air. She writes her name, and for half a second the letters float there. Then she holds it still. No ring. No letters. Just one small spitting point of light at the end of a wire. The circles never existed apart from that point. They were the point, moving. Gaudapada names the last section of the Mandukya Karika for nearly this picture, a burning stick from the fire, and today is the last day with him.
screen: `A SPARKLER IN THE DARK.` → `RINGS, LINES, A NAME.` → `HELD STILL: ONE POINT OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Karika's last section is called Alatashanti, the quieting of the firebrand. An alata is a burning stick, a torch pulled from the fire. Gaudapada says: when a firebrand is whirled, it appears straight, or crooked, or circling. In the same way, when consciousness moves, it appears as the one who perceives and the things perceived. When the firebrand is still, it is free of those shapes, and so is consciousness. Then he presses further. When the torch moves, the circles don't come into it from somewhere else. When it stops, they don't go off somewhere else, and they don't sink back inside it either. They were never things on their own. On his reading, the world of experience isn't a second thing standing apart from consciousness. It's how consciousness appears when it moves. Advaita teachers often reach for this picture to explain maya: the world isn't nothing, and it isn't fake; it just isn't a second thing apart from consciousness. He knows this is hard to hear. In this same section he speaks of a teaching that is deep and hard to see, and at the very end he salutes it, bowing as well as he is able. So the Karika ends not with an argument but with a bow. Advaita teachers count him as an early voice of their lineage, and tradition says he taught the teacher of Shankara. Other schools of Vedanta read the world as more fully real, with their own arguments.
screen: `ALATA: A BURNING STICK.` · `WHIRLED, IT DRAWS SHAPES.` · `THE SHAPES COME FROM NOWHERE ELSE.` · `THE KARIKA ENDS WITH A BOW.`

segments.voice: Watch the mind's motion, plans, pictures, bits of conversation, each one a shape the torch draws as it swings, without trying to stop any of it. Between them, look for a moment when the swinging slows and there is simply awareness, drawing nothing, and rest there as long as it lasts. If you pray, you can end by bowing your head, the way the Karika ends.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, which end with a torch held still and a bow to a truth he calls deep and hard to see.

1244.hook: a match struck in a dark kitchen. The Rig Veda's very first hymn begins with fire
1244.carry: agni, the fire, carries our offerings to the gods

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika ended: a firebrand whirled into circles, then held still, and a bow to a truth hard to see.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THE TORCH HELD STILL.`

segments.voice: Before dawn, in a dark kitchen, someone strikes a match. The scratch, the little flare, the smell of it. They touch it to a lamp's wick, or to the burner under the morning's tea, and the room changes. Faces appear. The kettle appears. The day has started. Fire is often the first thing awake in a house. So maybe it's no surprise where the Rig Veda begins. Not with a law, a list, or the making of the world. Its first hymn opens with a single name: Agni. The fire. Today, a new stretch of the path: the Vedas themselves.
screen: `A MATCH IN A DARK KITCHEN.` → `OFTEN THE FIRST THING AWAKE.` → `THE FIRST HYMN: AGNI.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. In the Sanskrit dictionaries, rig is a verse of praise, and veda is knowing. So the Rig Veda is knowledge carried in verses of praise. It's not a story told start to finish, and it's not a book of rules. It's a collection of hymns, made to be chanted aloud, addressed to many gods. And it opens with fire. In paraphrase, the first line says: I praise Agni, the household priest set in front, the god of the offering, the one who calls the gods, the richest giver of treasure. Notice the jobs piled onto one flame. Agni is the fire on the altar. He's the priest at the ritual. He calls out to the other gods and carries the offering up to them. Fire is the go-between, where earth and heaven meet. The next verse says seers old and new praise him. And the last verse turns tender. Be easy to reach, it asks Agni, as a father is to his son. Stay with us, for our good. That's why fire still stands at the heart of so many Hindu rites. In a havan, ghee and grain go into the flame, because Agni carries the offering to the gods. At a Hindu wedding, the couple walks around the sacred fire, with Agni as witness. And in many homes, a lamp is lit and waved before the deity at aarti. At the start of the Vedas, fire is the go-between. It still is.

1245.title: Heard, not written
1245.hook: say it after me: a song passed from one mouth to another, no page in sight. Tradition says the Rig Veda was heard, then carried by voice
1245.carry: the vedas are shruti: heard, and handed on by voice
1245.howItsDone: Vedic recitation is traditionally learned by ear from a teacher, the student repeating each phrase back, and chanters also learn recitation patterns that repeat and interweave the words to keep the sound exact.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rig Veda opened with Agni, praised and asked to be easy to reach, as a father is to his son. Agni, the fire, carries our offerings to the gods.
screen: `AGNI: THE FIRST HYMN.`

segments.voice: A grandmother sits on the edge of a bed and sings one line of an old song. The child sings it back, a little off. She sings it again, slower. The child tries again, and this time it lands. Next line. Nobody opens a book. The song moves from one mouth into one ear, and lives there now. Years later that child might sing it to someone else, the same way, line by line. Hindu tradition says the Rig Veda traveled this way, and it has a name for it.
screen: `SAY IT AFTER ME.` → `NO BOOK, NO PAGE.` → `MOUTH TO EAR.`

segments.voice: The Vedas are called shruti, what is heard. Tradition says the hymns weren't invented the way a song is written today. They were seen and heard by rishis, seers, in a kind of deep listening, then passed on by mouth, teacher to student. Tradition remembers each hymn with its seer, its god and its meter, so a chanter knows whose hymn it is and how it should sound. Some schools of interpretation, Mimamsa among them, go further: the Veda has no human author at all. The seers didn't make it; they received it. And yet the hymns sometimes speak of themselves another way. In one hymn to Agni the poet says, in paraphrase: I have fashioned this praise for you, as a skilled maker builds a chariot. Fitted, shaped, joined. So the tradition holds two pictures side by side: the hymn is heard, and the hymn is crafted with care. Some teachers hold them together: a seer can receive something and still work hard to say it well. That's why the sound matters so much. Vedic chanters learn the words not only straight through but in patterns that repeat and weave them, so a slip would be caught. The meaning matters, but in this tradition the sound itself is part of what's handed on. That's why a pandit at a havan may stop you over a single syllable: you've joined a long chain of voices.
screen: `SHRUTI: WHAT IS HEARD.` · `SEEN BY RISHIS, PASSED BY MOUTH.` · `CRAFTED LIKE A CHARIOT.` · `THE SOUND IS PART OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the room, the near sounds first, then the far ones, receiving them without naming or judging, the way a seer is said to receive a hymn. If a prayer or chant someone taught you by heart comes to mind, a shloka or a line of a bhajan, let it play quietly and notice whose voice it's in; if you pray, you can thank the people who carried words to you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vedas as shruti: heard, and handed on by voice, hymns carried mouth to ear, and a poet who fashioned his praise like a chariot.
screen: `SHRUTI: WHAT IS HEARD.`

segments.voice: At a family party, one woman answers to everything. Her kids call her Mom. Her nephew calls her Auntie. At the hospital that morning, her patients called her Doctor. Her granddaughter, toddling across the room, calls her something like Nani. Four names, and she turns her head for every one. Nobody is confused. Each name catches the side of her that person knows. Deep inside the Rig Veda, in a long and puzzling hymn, a verse says something very like this about the divine.
screen: `MOM, AUNTIE, DOCTOR, NANI.` → `ONE PERSON, MANY NAMES.` → `A VERSE DEEP IN THE RIG VEDA.`

segments.voice: The Rig Veda's hymns praise many gods. Agni, the fire. Indra, who wields the thunderbolt and frees the waters. Varuna, keeper of cosmic order. Mitra, the friend. Soma, the sacred drink. Ushas, the dawn. A hymn may praise its god in the highest terms, and another hymn may do the same for a different god. Then, in a long riddle-hymn, comes this verse. In paraphrase: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, and the heavenly bird with lovely wings. What is one, the wise speak of in many ways. They call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan. Ekam sat: one being, one truth, many names. Readers have heard it more than one way. Some hear all the gods as faces of one divine reality. Vedanta teachers later read it as pointing to Brahman. Others hear a poet's riddle about the sun, or about speech itself. The verse doesn't settle it. But it has become one of the most quoted lines in Hinduism. Many Hindus reach for it to explain why one family bows to Krishna, another to Shiva, another to the Goddess, and why they can honor the forms their neighbors love. And it fits the week: Gaudapada's one self that only seems many, then a fire, a voice, and now many names.
